definition:
The glory of God is the weight and radiance of who he is, made visible and known. Scripture uses the word in three related ways. It can mean God's own splendor, the fullness of his being and character, which belongs to him whether anyone sees it or not. It can mean that splendor shown to creatures, as when the glory of the LORD appears in the cloud and the fire of the wilderness or fills the tabernacle. And it can mean the honor creatures give back to God when they recognize who he is, as when the psalms call on the nations to ‘ascribe to the LORD glory’. The Bible also speaks of God sharing his glory with his people, so that the last stage of salvation is called glorification. The study of God's attributes traces his character, and the study of holiness and worship traces how a holy God makes a holy people; this study follows the visible, dwelling, radiant presence of God from the wilderness to the new Jerusalem.

The main Hebrew word is kabod. Its root is used for heaviness (the adjective kabed can mean ‘heavy’), and the noun covers a wide range: wealth (Laban's sons complain that Jacob has built ‘all this wealth’ out of their father's flocks, Genesis 31:1), honor and standing, and splendor (Joseph's ‘splendor in Egypt’, Genesis 45:13). Context, not the root, decides the sense in each place, but the range helps a reader hear what is meant when the word is used of God: substance, worth, and weight that shows. Other words stand near it: hod, ‘splendor’, hadar, ‘majesty’, and tiph'arah, ‘beauty’ or ‘glory’. In ordinary Greek the word doxa meant ‘opinion’ or ‘reputation’, but the translators of the Septuagint (the Greek Old Testament, made from about the third century BC onward) chose it for kabod, and so in the New Testament doxa carries the senses of radiance, majesty, and honor. The verb doxazō means ‘to glorify’, either to honor someone or to make their glory seen. Later Jewish writers, in the Aramaic Targums and the rabbinic literature, spoke of God's dwelling presence as the Shekinah, from the Hebrew shakan, ‘to dwell’. The word itself does not occur in the Bible, but the idea it names does.
ot:
Genesis does not use the word kabod of God, yet the creation it describes becomes in the rest of Scripture the first display of his glory. “The heavens declare the glory of God; the skies proclaim the work of His hands” (Psalm 19:1). Psalm 8 says God has “set Your glory above the heavens” and also that he has crowned human beings “with glory and honor” (Psalm 8:1, 5), a share in his splendor that fits their calling to rule the earth under him. Looking back, Stephen could say that “The God of glory appeared to our father Abraham” (Acts 7:2), but the word itself becomes a central theme only in Exodus.

In Exodus the glory of the LORD is a visible presence. In the wilderness, as Israel grumbles for food, “there in a cloud the glory of the LORD appeared” (Exodus 16:10). At Sinai “the glory of the LORD settled on Mount Sinai,” and to the people below it looked “like a consuming fire on the mountaintop” (Exodus 24:16-17). God tells Moses to build a sanctuary “so that I may dwell among them” (Exodus 25:8). After the golden calf Moses asks, “Please show me Your glory” (Exodus 33:18), and God answers that he will make his goodness pass by and proclaim his name, but “You cannot see My face, for no one can see Me and live” (Exodus 33:20). Glory here is not only brightness. It is God's character, his name and his goodness, displayed. When the tabernacle is finished, “the glory of the LORD filled the tabernacle” so fully that Moses could not enter (Exodus 40:34-35). The same glory appears at the first sacrifices (Leviticus 9:23-24) and in judgment at the people's rebellion (Numbers 14:10). There, as God pardons the people yet bars that generation from the land, he swears “as surely as the whole earth is filled with the glory of the LORD” (Numbers 14:21), the first statement of a horizon wider than Israel's camp.

The glory can be lost from view. When the Philistines captured the ark, the priest Eli's widowed daughter-in-law named her son Ichabod, a name usually understood as ‘Where is the glory?’ or ‘No glory’, saying, “The glory has departed from Israel” (1 Samuel 4:21). When Solomon dedicated the temple in Jerusalem, the cloud filled it and “the glory of the LORD filled the house of the LORD” so that the priests could not stand to minister (1 Kings 8:10-11; compare 2 Chronicles 7:1-3). Israel's worship then answered the glory. The psalms call the LORD “the King of Glory” (Psalm 24:7-10) and summon heavenly beings and the families of the nations to “Ascribe to the LORD the glory due His name” (Psalm 29:2; 96:7-8). They also refuse to share it: “Not to us, O LORD, not to us, but to Your name be the glory” (Psalm 115:1). Idolatry is described as a trade. At Horeb Israel “exchanged their Glory for the image of a grass-eating ox” (Psalm 106:20), and Jeremiah charges that God's people “have exchanged their Glory for useless idols” (Jeremiah 2:11).

The prophets carry the theme into judgment and hope. In the year King Uzziah died (around 740 BC), Isaiah saw the Lord enthroned and heard the seraphim cry, “Holy, holy, holy is the LORD of Hosts; all the earth is full of His glory” (Isaiah 6:3). Later chapters of Isaiah promise that “the glory of the LORD will be revealed, and all humanity together will see it” (Isaiah 40:5), insist “I will not yield My glory to another or My praise to idols” (Isaiah 42:8), say that God's people were “created for My glory” (Isaiah 43:7), and picture the nations coming to Zion's light as “the glory of the LORD rises upon you” (Isaiah 60:1-3). Ezekiel, a priest among the exiles in Babylon, saw the glory by the River Kebar and fell on his face (Ezekiel 1:28). In a vision dated to about 592 BC he watched it leave: from the cherubim to the threshold of the temple (Ezekiel 9:3), to the east gate (Ezekiel 10:18-19), and finally out of the city to the mountain on its east (Ezekiel 11:22-23). The temple fell in 587 or 586 BC with its glory already gone. In a later vision, about 573 BC, Ezekiel saw “the glory of the God of Israel coming from the east,” and “the glory of the LORD filled the temple” (Ezekiel 43:2-5); the book ends by naming the city “THE LORD IS THERE” (Ezekiel 48:35).

After the exile the promise stays open. The second temple was dedicated with joy (Ezra 6:16), but the Old Testament records no cloud filling it as one had filled Solomon's. Haggai promised that “The latter glory of this house will be greater than the former” (Haggai 2:9), and Zechariah heard God say of Jerusalem, “I will be the glory within it” (Zechariah 2:5). Habakkuk gave the hope its widest form: “the earth will be filled with the knowledge of the glory of the LORD as the waters cover the sea” (Habakkuk 2:14), echoing Isaiah 11:9.
nt:
The New Testament opens with the glory returning. On the night of Jesus' birth “the glory of the Lord shone around” the shepherds, and the angels sang, “Glory to God in the highest” (Luke 2:9, 14). John states the whole claim in one sentence: “The Word became flesh and made His dwelling among us. We have seen His glory, the glory of the one and only Son from the Father, full of grace and truth” (John 1:14). The verb for ‘made His dwelling’, eskēnōsen, is related to skēnē, ‘tent’, the word the Septuagint used for the tabernacle, so many readers hear in it the tabernacle where the glory once settled. Where Moses was told that no one could see God's face and live, John says that “the one and only Son, who is Himself God and is at the Father's side, has made Him known” (John 1:18). Jesus' signs reveal his glory (John 2:11), he speaks of his body as the temple (John 2:19-21), and John says that Isaiah, in the vision of Isaiah 6, “saw Jesus' glory and spoke about Him” (John 12:41). At the transfiguration Jesus' face “shone like the sun” (Matthew 17:2); Luke says the disciples “saw Jesus' glory” as Moses and Elijah spoke with him about his coming departure at Jerusalem (Luke 9:31-32), and 2 Peter recalls the voice from “the Majestic Glory” (2 Peter 1:17).

John's Gospel then says something unexpected: the fullest display of glory is the cross. When Greeks come asking to see him, Jesus says, “The hour has come for the Son of Man to be glorified,” and at once speaks of a kernel of wheat that must fall to the ground and die (John 12:23-24). When Judas goes out to betray him, Jesus says, “Now the Son of Man is glorified, and God is glorified in Him” (John 13:31). In his prayer before the arrest he asks, “glorify Me in Your presence with the glory I had with You before the world existed” (John 17:5), a glory that belongs to the Son eternally, and he prays that his people will be with him “that they may see the glory You gave Me” (John 17:24). Paul calls the crucified one “the Lord of glory” (1 Corinthians 2:8), and Hebrews says that the Son is “the radiance of God's glory and the exact representation of His nature” (Hebrews 1:3). In the New Testament, God's glory has a face and a history.

Paul sets the whole human story inside the theme. Humanity “exchanged the glory of the immortal God for images of mortal man and birds and animals and reptiles” (Romans 1:23), echoing Psalm 106:20, so that “all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God” (Romans 3:23). Salvation restores what was lost: believers “rejoice in the hope of the glory of God” (Romans 5:2), present sufferings are not comparable “to the glory that will be revealed in us” (Romans 8:18), creation itself waits to share “the glorious freedom of the children of God” (Romans 8:21), and those God justified “He also glorified” (Romans 8:30). In 2 Corinthians 3 Paul contrasts the glory on Moses' face, which faded, with believers who “with unveiled faces all reflect the glory of the Lord” and are “being transformed into His image with intensifying glory” (2 Corinthians 3:18). The God who said “Let light shine out of darkness” has given “the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ” (2 Corinthians 4:6), a deliberate echo of Genesis 1:3. Present affliction produces “an eternal weight of glory” (2 Corinthians 4:17); Paul sets the Greek word for weight, baros, beside doxa, and many commentators hear in the pairing the Hebrew sense of kabod.

The apostles also speak of glory as the goal of the Christian's ordinary life. Salvation is “to the praise of His glory” (Ephesians 1:12, 14), and Christ in his people is “the hope of glory” (Colossians 1:27). Believers are to “glorify God with your body” (1 Corinthians 6:20) and to do everything, eating and drinking included, “to the glory of God” (1 Corinthians 10:31). Peter tells suffering Christians that “the Spirit of glory and of God rests on you” (1 Peter 4:14). Herod Agrippa's death is told as the fate of a ruler who “did not give glory to God” (Acts 12:23). The letters overflow with doxologies, short outbursts of praise such as “To Him be the glory forever” (Romans 11:36) and Jude's closing ascription of glory, majesty, dominion, and authority (Jude 1:25).

The end of the story is glory seen and shared. The Son of Man will come “in His Father's glory with the holy angels” (Mark 8:38), and Christians await the “glorious appearance of our great God and Savior Jesus Christ” (Titus 2:13). The body sown in dishonor “is raised in glory” (1 Corinthians 15:43), conformed to “His glorious body” (Philippians 3:21). Revelation gathers the Old Testament threads. The heavenly court sings that God is worthy “to receive glory and honor and power, for You created all things” (Revelation 4:11). The heavenly temple fills with smoke from the glory of God so that no one can enter (Revelation 15:8), as the tabernacle once did. In the new Jerusalem John sees no temple, “because the Lord God Almighty and the Lamb are its temple,” and “the glory of God illuminates the city, and the Lamb is its lamp” (Revelation 21:22-23). The kings of the earth bring their glory into it (Revelation 21:24-26), and the request Moses was refused is finally granted: “They will see His face” (Revelation 22:4).

keyTexts.why: Moses asks to see God's glory and is shown his goodness and his name, but not his face. Glory is God's character made known, and full sight of it waits.
The glory of the LORD fills the finished tabernacle. The God of Sinai comes to dwell in the middle of his people's camp.
In the middle of Israel's rebellion God swears by the filling of the whole earth with his glory. The first statement of the universal horizon.
At the ark's capture a child is named Ichabod because the glory has departed. Israel learns that the presence can be lost from view.
The cloud and the glory fill Solomon's temple so that the priests cannot minister. The high point of God's dwelling in Israel's history.
The heavens declare the glory of God without speech or language. Creation itself is a witness to his splendor.
The seraphim cry that the whole earth is full of the LORD's glory. John later says Isaiah saw Christ's glory here.
The glory leaves the threshold of the temple before Jerusalem falls. Judgment is described as God's departure.
The glory returns from the east and fills the temple. The promise that God will again dwell among his people.
The earth will be filled with the knowledge of the glory of the LORD as the waters cover the sea. The Old Testament's widest statement of the hope.
The Word became flesh and pitched his tent among us, and his glory was seen. The glory of the tabernacle now dwells in a human life.
Jesus asks the Father to glorify him with the glory he had before the world existed, at the hour of the cross. The Son's glory is eternal, and it is revealed in his death.
All have sinned and fall short of the glory of God. Sin is described as the loss of the glory humanity was made to reflect.
Believers behold the Lord's glory with unveiled faces and are transformed, because God has shone the knowledge of his glory in the face of Jesus Christ.
The new Jerusalem needs no temple and no sun, because God and the Lamb are its temple and its light. The glory fills everything.

history:
The early church spoke of glory first in its worship. Christian prayer from the start ended in doxologies patterned on the New Testament's, ascribing glory to the Father through the Son and in the Spirit, and in the controversies of the fourth century the form of the doxology itself became a way of confessing that the Son and the Spirit share the Father's glory; Basil of Caesarea's treatise On the Holy Spirit (around 375) defended giving glory to the Father with the Son together with the Spirit. Irenaeus of Lyons, writing against the Gnostics around 180, taught that God's glory is displayed in a living human being and that human life consists in the vision of God, a pairing that joins God's glory and human flourishing instead of setting them against each other. In the Arian controversy, Athanasius and the Nicene party used the image of Hebrews 1:3, the radiance that is never separate from the light, to argue that the Son is eternally one with the Father, and the Creed of Nicaea (325) confessed him as ‘Light from Light’.

East and West developed the hope of seeing God's glory in different vocabularies. In the West, Augustine closed The City of God (completed around 426) with the saints' eternal rest in the sight of God. Thomas Aquinas, in the Summa Theologiae (begun around 1265), taught that the blessed see the essence of God, not by natural power, but by a created ‘light of glory’ given to the mind, and Pope Benedict XII's constitution Benedictus Deus (1336) defined that the souls of the saints see the divine essence face to face. In the East, the feast of the Transfiguration gave the theme a liturgical center. In the fourteenth century the monk Gregory Palamas, later archbishop of Thessalonica, defended the hesychasts, monks who prayed in stillness and claimed to see a divine light. He taught that the light seen on Mount Tabor was God's own uncreated energy, truly God, while God's essence remains beyond all creatures. Councils at Constantinople between 1341 and 1351 upheld his teaching, and it became standard in Eastern Orthodox theology.

The Reformation made the glory of God a watchword. ‘Soli Deo gloria’, to God alone be the glory, is often listed with the other Reformation slogans, though the familiar set of five is a later way of summarizing them; Johann Sebastian Bach wrote the initials S.D.G. at the end of many of his manuscripts. Martin Luther's Heidelberg Disputation (1518) set a ‘theology of the cross’, which finds God hidden in the suffering and shame of Christ, against a ‘theology of glory’, which looks for him in visible power and success. John Calvin, in the Institutes (final edition 1559), repeatedly described the created world as a theater of God's glory. The Westminster Shorter Catechism (1647) opens by answering that humanity's chief end is to glorify God and to enjoy him forever, joining the two as one purpose. Roman Catholic spirituality has its own form of the watchword in the motto of the Society of Jesus, founded by Ignatius of Loyola and approved in 1540: ad maiorem Dei gloriam, for the greater glory of God. John Owen's Meditations and Discourses on the Glory of Christ, published in 1684 just after his death, urged Christians to contemplate God's glory in the person of Christ now as a foretaste of heaven.

Jonathan Edwards gave the doctrine one of its most influential modern statements in his Dissertation Concerning the End for Which God Created the World, published in 1765, seven years after his death. He argued that God created the world to communicate his own fullness, so that his glory going out to creatures and their knowing, loving, and rejoicing in him are one end, not two. In the twentieth century Karl Barth, in Church Dogmatics II/1 (1940), treated God's glory as the last of the divine perfections and discussed it in terms of God's beauty, and the Swiss Catholic theologian Hans Urs von Balthasar built a multi-volume theology around it, The Glory of the Lord (Herrlichkeit, 1961 to 1969), arguing that theology should begin with the beauty of God's self-revelation in Christ. The site does not yet have a separate systematic page on this doctrine; related treatments are at /theology/doctrine/divine-attributes and /theology/doctrine/last-things.

differ.view: Seeing God's essence: the beatific vision
differ.body: In the life to come the redeemed will see God himself, not a created image or a sign of him. Defenders in the Western tradition, from Augustine to Thomas Aquinas and in Roman Catholic teaching since Benedictus Deus (1336), and with variations in much Protestant theology, point to texts such as Matthew 5:8, 1 Corinthians 13:12, 1 John 3:2, and Revelation 22:4, which promise sight ‘face to face’. No creature can reach this by its own power; God lifts the mind by grace so that it can know him directly, while never comprehending him fully. They argue that anything less than God himself would leave the human heart, made for God, still restless, and that the promises of Scripture are plainly promises of God, not of something that stands in for him.

differ.view: Participating in God's energies: the Orthodox account
differ.body: God's essence, what God is in himself, remains beyond every creature forever, even in glory, but God truly gives himself in his uncreated energies, which are not created effects but God himself acting and shining. Defenders, following Gregory Palamas and the fourteenth-century councils at Constantinople, point to the light of the transfiguration, the promise that believers become “partakers of the divine nature” (2 Peter 1:4), and texts such as John 1:18 and 1 Timothy 6:16 that say no one has seen or can see God. They argue that this distinction alone protects both God's transcendence and a real union with him, which the Orthodox call theosis (deification), and that the saints will grow into God's glory without end.

differ.view: Seeing God's glory in the face of Christ
differ.body: Many Reformed writers, drawing on John Owen's Meditations and Discourses on the Glory of Christ (1684), stress that the vision of God is always mediated through the incarnate Son. Now by faith and then by sight, believers behold “the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ” (2 Corinthians 4:6), and Jesus prays that his people will be with him to see his glory (John 17:24). Defenders do not deny that the redeemed will know God truly, but they hold that the Son's glorified humanity will not be set aside as a ladder once climbed; the Lamb is the city's lamp (Revelation 21:23). They argue that this keeps the vision of God tied to the gospel and to the particular person of Jesus rather than to a general idea of the divine.

errors:
The church has rejected several misreadings of God's glory. One treats God's concern for his glory as vanity, as though God needed praise to feel secure or were a performer craving applause. Scripture says God is not served “as if He needed anything” (Acts 17:25); his glory is not a lack he fills from creatures but a fullness he shares with them. The theologians who have written most about God seeking his glory, from Irenaeus to Edwards, have insisted that God's glory and his creatures' good are not rivals. A second error confuses the glory that fills the earth with the earth itself, as pantheism does. Isaiah hears that the earth is full of God's glory, not that the earth is God; the glory is God's presence and display in his world, and he remains its Creator and Lord.

A third distortion is what Luther called a theology of glory: looking for God chiefly in power, success, and visible triumph, and expecting his people to share his glory without sharing Christ's sufferings. The New Testament ties them together (Romans 8:17-18; 1 Peter 4:13), and the Gospel of John names the cross as the hour of glory. Prosperity teaching, which promises health and wealth as the visible sign of God's favor, is a modern form of this error. The last is the oldest: idolatry, which the Bible describes as exchanging God's glory for something smaller (Psalm 106:20; Romans 1:23). Giving to a nation, a leader, a movement, or oneself the glory that belongs to God is the same exchange in a new setting, and Scripture treats it as a matter of the first seriousness.
life:
The doctrine of glory gives the smallest parts of life a direction. Paul's instruction to eat and drink to the glory of God (1 Corinthians 10:31) means that ordinary work, meals, and rest are places where God's goodness can be recognized and thanked. It also frees a person from a heavy burden. Jesus asked how people could believe while they “accept glory from one another” (John 5:44); a life spent seeking honor from others is exhausting and fragile, and the call to give glory to God releases a person from needing to be the center. Prayer begins here, with “hallowed be Your name” (Matthew 6:9), asking that God be known as he is before asking for anything else.

Glory also shapes hope in suffering. Paul called his afflictions “light and momentary” only by setting them beside an eternal weight of glory (2 Corinthians 4:17), and he did not pretend they were light in themselves. The Christian hope is not only relief but sight: to see God's face in Christ and to be changed by the seeing. That hope makes worship a rehearsal for what is coming, and it gives every believer, however obscure, a share in the purpose for which the world was made.
questions: The glory of the LORD fills the tabernacle, leaves the temple in Ezekiel, and is seen in Jesus according to John 1:14. What does this storyline suggest about where God chooses to make his glory known?
John's Gospel calls the cross the hour of Jesus' glorification. How does that change what the word glory means, and how might it correct ideas of glory that measure it by success or power?
Paul says to eat and drink to the glory of God. What would it look like to do an ordinary task this week in that way, and what would have to change in your motives?
